main moves past it, on the same head commit, with no push from the author. The
rule is not reimplemented: it runs `scripts/check-migration-order.sh` with
`BASE_REF=origin/main`, from a copy taken before any PR tree is checked out.

The verdict comes from the PR's **merge** ref, not its head — "would the
migrations be in order if this merged right now" — and is reported on the head
commit, which is what a ruleset evaluates. Judging the head instead would trip
the max-decrease guard on any branch that simply hasn't merged main in.

Reporting is all it does until `migration-order` is added to
`required_status_checks` on the repo-level `main` ruleset (id `18407568`, which
today requires `test` alone with `strict_required_status_checks_policy: false`).
That is one repo-admin edit, and a smaller one than turning on strict mode,
which would force every open PR to rebase. Once required, the merge is blocked
rather than merely flagged.

Do it after one push to main has run the recheck: that pass marks every open PR,
including those touching no migrations, so no PR is left waiting on a context
that never reports. One gap survives: a PR from a fork has a read-only token and
cannot post its own status, so once the context is required someone has to post
it by hand. The workflow logs a warning saying so.

`scripts/recheck_open_migration_prs_test.go` covers the recheck the way
`check_migration_order_test.go` covers the check — real git against throwaway
repos, with `gh` stubbed and merge refs written as `refs/pull/N/merge`.

### Merged is not applied

A migration on `main` has not necessarily run anywhere: when `migration-check`
blocks a deploy, the file sits on `main` and no database ever sees it. The
"never renumber a merged migration" rule is about *applied* migrations, and
re-stamping is the fix for the merged-but-unapplied case — the deploy stays
blocked until the version moves.

`refs/deploy/staging` is the answer: `git fetch origin refs/deploy/staging` and
check whether the file is in that tree. To confirm against a real database, ask
the catalog for the object the migration creates:

```sql
SELECT to_regclass('repo.<table>');
```

Not `information_schema.tables`, which lists only objects the reading role holds
a privilege on — `repo_secret_kv` revokes `SELECT` from `operator_ro`, so it
reads as absent there even when applied. Not `goose_activity_repo` either:
`026_operator_iam_roles.sql` grants the operator roles nothing outside schema
`repo`, and goose creates its version table unqualified, so `operator_ro` gets
`permission denied`. There is a cluster per region (staging `us-west-2`,
`eu-west-1`, `us-east-2`; prod `us-east-2`, `eu-central-1`, `ap-southeast-2`,
`ap-south-1`), each with its own version table.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
#MISE description="Run store + sessionname + importer integration tests against a throwaway Postgres; pass packages to run only those, in full"
set -euo pipefail

project_root="${MISE_PROJECT_ROOT:-$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)}"
# shellcheck source=scripts/test-resources.sh
source "$project_root/scripts/test-resources.sh"
pg_name="$(test_resource_name activity-pg-test)"

cleanup() { docker rm -f "$pg_name" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true; }
trap cleanup EXIT
cleanup

docker run --rm --name "$pg_name" -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=REDACTED -p 127.0.0.1::5432 -d postgres:16 \
  "${TEST_PG_DURABILITY_FLAGS[@]}"
pg_port="$(test_resource_port "$pg_name" 5432)"
echo "Waiting for Postgres..."
pg_ready=0
for _ in $(seq 1 30); do
  if docker exec "$pg_name" pg_isready -U postgres >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    pg_ready=1
    break
  fi
  sleep 1
done
if [ "$pg_ready" -ne 1 ]; then
  echo "Postgres ($pg_name) did not become ready within 30s; last logs:" >&2
  docker logs --tail 20 "$pg_name" >&2 || true
  exit 1
fi
# internal/sessionname carries the AI namer's prompt-resolution chain test (real
# store query → checkpoint layout → Repo API read). It cannot live in internal/store:
# sessionname imports store, so an in-package store test importing it back is an
# import cycle. internal/runnerschedulereconcile is here for the same reason
# (it imports store). -p 1 because all four packages migrate the same physical
# database.
#
# internal/importer's TestIntegration* tests self-skip without
# ACTIVITY_TEST_DATABASE_URL, and until ENT-1458 no task set it for that package —
# so the whole PlanetScale-importer integration suite ran nowhere, and a stale
# assertion (the ENT-1165 warning ENT-1165 itself deleted) sat red unnoticed. Its
# blob-backed cases use the in-memory fakes, so plain Postgres is all it needs; the
# MinIO-backed attachments test lives in test:attachments.
#
# With no arguments this runs the full default set, as it always has. With
# arguments it runs exactly those named packages in full rather than filtered
# by -run Integration: that pattern assumes tests are named TestIntegration*,
# which not every package follows — cmd/import-planetscale's are TestRun*, so
# the filter would make it pass having executed nothing. A change whose blast
# radius is one package stops paying for four.
dsn="REDACTED"
if [ "$#" -gt 0 ]; then
  ACTIVITY_TEST_DATABASE_URL="$dsn" \
    go test "$@" -p 1 -v -timeout 20m
  exit 0
fi

ACTIVITY_TEST_DATABASE_URL="$dsn" \
  go test ./internal/store/ ./internal/sessionname/ ./internal/importer/ ./internal/runnerschedulereconcile/ -run Integration -p 1 -v -timeout 20m

# cmd/import-planetscale's RunState tests are DB-backed too (openRepoStoreForRunState,
# same env var) but named TestRun*, so -run Integration would skip them even with the
# DSN set — they ran nowhere for the same reason internal/importer did. No -run filter
# here: the package's other tests are cheap pure-Go ones that are fine to run twice.
ACTIVITY_TEST_DATABASE_URL="$dsn" \
  go test ./cmd/import-planetscale/ -p 1 -v -timeout 20m

---
name: using-entire
description: >
  Use for any codebase exploration or understanding task — reads historical
  intent from Entire checkpoints instead of guessing. Orchestrates other Entire
  skills to give the agent provenance-backed answers about code.
---

# Using Entire

Your default when exploring or understanding code should be: **read the
recorded intent, don't guess.**

Entire checkpoints capture the prompts, transcripts, and decisions behind every
agent-driven change. When you need to understand why code exists or how a module
evolved, look up the checkpoint history first. Only fall back to inference from
code structure when no history is available — and label that explicitly.

## When This Skill Activates

Use this skill whenever the task involves:

- Exploring or understanding an unfamiliar module or file
- Preparing to refactor, extend, or debug code you didn't write
- Answering "why is this like this?" or "what was the intent?"
- Doing pre-work research before making changes
- Any codebase exploration where historical context would help

Do **not** use this skill for simple, well-understood edits where you already
have full context (e.g. "add a comment to line 5").

## First Step: Check Repository Status

Before diving into specific lookups, check whether Entire is available and
the repository has checkpoint history:

```bash
entire status
```

This tells you whether Entire is enabled, which git hooks are installed, whether
the metadata branch is initialized, and any active sessions on the current
branch.

## Scenario Routing

When this skill activates, determine which sub-skill best fits the user's need:

| Scenario | Typical user expressions | Delegate to |
|----------|------------------------|-------------|
| Code block provenance | "why is this like this" / "wtf is going on" / "what happened at src/auth.ts:42" / "tell me why this changed" | `what-happened` |
| Find prior work | "has anyone done X before" / "search past work for rate limiting" / "find the previous implementation" | `search` |
| Recall a task playbook | "have we done this before" / "recall how we did X" / "how did we do this last time" | `recall` |
| Replay feature history | "replay <feature>" / "walk me through how X was built" / "show me the journey of Y" | `replay` |
| Teach a repo topic | "teach me <topic>" / "how does <topic> work in this repo" / "give me a lesson on X" | `teach` |
| Understand original intent | "explain this function" / "explain parseConfig" / "what was the intent behind src/auth.ts" | `explain` |
| Generate a dispatch / summary | "summarize recent work" / "generate a dispatch" / "what was accomplished this week" | run `entire dispatch` directly |
| Code review with intent context | "review these changes" / "review this branch" / "audit before merging" | `review` |
| Hand off to another agent | "hand off this session" / "continue in another agent" / "pick up the codex session" | `session-handoff` |
| Convert session to skill | "turn this into a skill" / "make a skill from this session" | `session-to-skill` |
| Link session to other repos | "link session to other repos" / "attach session to the foo repo" | `session-crosslink` |
| General exploration | "understand this module" / "explore how auth works" / "help me understand the codebase" | _(self — see below)_ |

If the scenario clearly maps to a sub-skill, delegate entirely to that skill's
workflow. Do not duplicate their steps here.

## General Exploration Flow

When no specific sub-skill fits — e.g. the user asks to "understand this
module" or "explore how auth works" — use this flow:

1. **Identify key files** in the target area (entry points, main types, core
   functions).

2. **Check for checkpoint coverage** on each key file:

```bash
git log --format='%H %s' -5 -- <file>
```

Look for `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailers in the commit bodies:

```bash
git log --format='%H %b' -5 -- <file> | grep -B1 'Entire-Checkpoint:'
```

3. **Read intent for covered commits** — extract the checkpoint ID from the
   trailer, then use JSON output for non-interactive consumption:

```bash
entire checkpoint explain --checkpoint <checkpoint-id> --json --no-pager
```

If you only have a commit hash (not a checkpoint ID), use:

```bash
entire checkpoint explain --commit <sha> --no-pager
```

4. **Synthesize**: combine the recorded intent (from checkpoints) with the
   current code structure to build a comprehensive understanding.

5. **Report** your findings, clearly distinguishing:
   - Facts backed by checkpoint transcripts (label as "recorded intent")
   - Observations inferred from code alone (label as "inferred from code")

## AI Agent Usage Notes

When running Entire commands from an agent subprocess:

- **Always pass `--json`** for commands that support it and might prompt
  interactively. `--json` implies non-interactive output.
- **Always pass `--no-pager`** to prevent pager activation in subprocess
  contexts.
- **Always specify `--checkpoint <id>` or `--commit <sha>`** for
  `entire checkpoint explain` — without a locator, the command falls back to an
  interactive picker.

## When No Checkpoints Exist

If the target code predates Entire or has no checkpoint coverage:

1. Say explicitly: "No Entire checkpoint history is available for this code."
2. Proceed with standard code understanding (read source, check git log, trace
   call sites).
3. Label all explanations as "inferred from code — not backed by recorded
   intent."
4. If the user wants deeper history, suggest `search` with related keywords —
   there may be checkpoints on related work even if the specific file isn't
   directly covered.

## Transparency Principle

Always make it clear whether your answer comes from:

- **Checkpoint-backed history** — you read the actual session transcript and
  know the developer's stated intent
- **Code inference** — you analyzed the code structure and are reasoning about
  probable intent

Never present inferred intent as if it were recorded fact. The core value of
this workflow is that distinction.

## References

For a deeper understanding of Entire's capabilities beyond what the sub-skills
cover, consult these resources:

- **CLI help**: run `entire help` to see all available commands and flags
- **Documentation**: https://docs.entire.io/llms.txt — AI-friendly
  documentation index following the [llms.txt standard](https://llmstxt.org),
  designed to be consumed directly by LLMs and coding agents
Entire's CLI is the source of truth for its own usage. Do not guess flags or
subcommands — read them from this command. You are already inside the repo:
entire auto-detects it from the git origin remote, so never ask the user for the
repo name. Pass --repo only to target a DIFFERENT repo.

Current repo: gh/entireio/cli  (auto-detected from origin; pass --repo only for a DIFFERENT repo)

When to use entire — the commands that bear on the work:
  checkpoint  Inspect and search checkpoints
                read-only except: policy
  search      Search checkpoints, commits, and sessions using semantic and keyword matching
                read-only
  session     Manage agent sessions tracked by Entire
                read-only except: adopt, attach, resume, stop
  status      Show Entire status
                read-only
  trail       Manage trails for your branches
                read-only: approvals, list, show, watch — others write
  why         Show why a line exists
                read-only

Also available (entire agent-help <command> for any of these):
  read-only, safe to run:
    activity · blame · experts · labs · recap · tokens · version
  when the task needs them:
    api · dispatch · doctor · import · runner
  the user's — suggest, don't run:
    agent · auth · clean · configure · disable · enable · grant
    investigate · login · logout · org · plugin · project · repo
    review

Drill in for exact, currently-installed flags:  entire agent-help <command>  (e.g. entire agent-help trail)
Add --json for structured output.
a9a676e79 2026-08-14 refactor(hooks)!: remove local_dev mode
Local-dev mode pointed installed hooks at `scripts/entire-dev`, a launcher
inside the working tree that compiled and ran the checked-out source. It was
read from the *committed* `.entire/settings.json` (settings.go merged
`local_dev` from the project scope, and strategy/common.go regenerated the git
hook from it), so any repository could commit `"local_dev": true` and have
`entire enable` install hooks that execute that repository's own code. A branch
checkout could then swap what ran. This repo shipped exactly that: `local_dev:
true` was tracked, and all six committed agent configs invoked the launcher.

Hooks now always name the `entire` binary. Removed the `--local-dev` flags
(including the non-hidden one on `entire agent add`), `EnableOptions.LocalDev`,
the `localDev` parameter from `Agent.InstallHooks` across all nine agents and
the external-agent protocol, the claude-code local-dev SessionEnd timeout, and
the launcher script.

`EntireSettings.LocalDev` stays as a documented no-op: the loaders use
DisallowUnknownFields, so deleting the field would make every existing settings
file containing `local_dev` a hard parse error. It is not merged from overrides
and nothing reads it, matching the `Strategy` precedent.

Removing the feature is not enough to disarm existing installs, so this also
fixes how hooks written by older versions get replaced:

- `isGitHookInstalledInHooksDir` only looked for the Entire marker, which a
  legacy hook still carries. It therefore read as installed forever and
  EnsureSetup never reinstalled it — while the script it invoked no longer
  existed. Repo-relative prefixes got no availability guard and pre-push
  deliberately propagates exit codes, so that state rejects `git push`. A hook
  naming the legacy launcher now counts as not installed.
- claudecode, factoryaidroid and copilotcli only dropped Entire hooks under
  `--force`, so a plain enable added the current hook beside the legacy one and
  both fired. cursor and codex returned early whenever the current command was
  present, leaving a legacy hook next to it. Stale hooks are now dropped on
  every install, through one shared `agent.DropStaleManagedHooks` primitive
  rather than six per-agent re-derivations (`dupl` cannot see duplication across
  packages, which is how the two divergent copies survived).
- geminicli's idempotency check sampled only SessionStart, so a stale hook on
  any of the other ten types survived every non-force install.
- The write now happens when only a drop occurred: a config can hold both a
  stale and a current hook, where nothing needs adding.
- Every hook prefix is guarded by an existence test. The unguarded path existed
  only for the repo-relative launcher, and was still reachable for unusual
  absolute paths — exactly where losing the guard hurts most.

Regenerates this repo's six committed agent configs through the real install
path. The pi extension had also drifted far enough to be missing the
ENTIRE_PI_NESTED subagent guard that was already in its template, so
`testutil.AssertCommittedDogfoodFile` and `AssertCommittedDogfoodConfigStable`
now fail in CI on drift instead of waiting for someone to notice.

have full context (e.g. "add a comment to line 5").

name: using-entire
description: >
  Use for any codebase exploration or understanding task — reads historical
  intent from Entire checkpoints instead of guessing. Orchestrates other Entire
  skills to give the agent provenance-backed answers about code.
---

# Using Entire

Your default when exploring or understanding code should be: **read the
recorded intent, don't guess.**

Entire checkpoints capture the prompts, transcripts, and decisions behind every
agent-driven change. When you need to understand why code exists or how a module
evolved, look up the checkpoint history first. Only fall back to inference from
code structure when no history is available — and label that explicitly.

## When This Skill Activates

Use this skill whenever the task involves:

- Exploring or understanding an unfamiliar module or file
- Preparing to refactor, extend, or debug code you didn't write
- Answering "why is this like this?" or "what was the intent?"
- Doing pre-work research before making changes
- Any codebase exploration where historical context would help

Do **not** use this skill for simple, well-understood edits where you already
have full context (e.g. "add a comment to line 5").

## First Step: Check Repository Status

Before diving into specific lookups, check whether Entire is available and
the repository has checkpoint history:

```bash
entire status
```

This tells you whether Entire is enabled, which git hooks are installed, whether
the metadata branch is initialized, and any active sessions on the current
branch.

## Scenario Routing

When this skill activates, determine which sub-skill best fits the user's need:

| Scenario | Typical user expressions | Delegate to |
|----------|------------------------|-------------|
| Code block provenance | "why is this like this" / "wtf is going on" / "what happened at src/auth.ts:42" / "tell me why this changed" | `what-happened` |
| Find prior work | "has anyone done X before" / "search past work for rate limiting" / "find the previous implementation" | `search` |
| Recall a task playbook | "have we done this before" / "recall how we did X" / "how did we do this last time" | `recall` |
| Replay feature history | "replay <feature>" / "walk me through how X was built" / "show me the journey of Y" | `replay` |
| Teach a repo topic | "teach me <topic>" / "how does <topic> work in this repo" / "give me a lesson on X" | `teach` |
| Understand original intent | "explain this function" / "explain parseConfig" / "what was the intent behind src/auth.ts" | `explain` |
| Generate a dispatch / summary | "summarize recent work" / "generate a dispatch" / "what was accomplished this week" | run `entire dispatch` directly |
| Code review with intent context | "review these changes" / "review this branch" / "audit before merging" | `review` |
| Hand off to another agent | "hand off this session" / "continue in another agent" / "pick up the codex session" | `session-handoff` |
| Convert session to skill | "turn this into a skill" / "make a skill from this session" | `session-to-skill` |
| Link session to other repos | "link session to other repos" / "attach session to the foo repo" | `session-crosslink` |
| General exploration | "understand this module" / "explore how auth works" / "help me understand the codebase" | _(self — see below)_ |

If the scenario clearly maps to a sub-skill, delegate entirely to that skill's
workflow. Do not duplicate their steps here.

## General Exploration Flow

When no specific sub-skill fits — e.g. the user asks to "understand this
module" or "explore how auth works" — use this flow:

1. **Identify key files** in the target area (entry points, main types, core
   functions).

2. **Check for checkpoint coverage** on each key file:

```bash
git log --format='%H %s' -5 -- <file>
```

Look for `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailers in the commit bodies:

```bash
git log --format='%H %b' -5 -- <file> | grep -B1 'Entire-Checkpoint:'
```

3. **Read intent for covered commits** — extract the checkpoint ID from the
   trailer, then use JSON output for non-interactive consumption:

```bash
entire checkpoint explain --checkpoint <checkpoint-id> --json --no-pager
```

If you only have a commit hash (not a checkpoint ID), use:

```bash
entire checkpoint explain --commit <sha> --no-pager
```

4. **Synthesize**: combine the recorded intent (from checkpoints) with the
   current code structure to build a comprehensive understanding.

5. **Report** your findings, clearly distinguishing:
   - Facts backed by checkpoint transcripts (label as "recorded intent")
   - Observations inferred from code alone (label as "inferred from code")

## AI Agent Usage Notes

When running Entire commands from an agent subprocess:

- **Always pass `--json`** for commands that support it and might prompt
  interactively. `--json` implies non-interactive output.
- **Always pass `--no-pager`** to prevent pager activation in subprocess
  contexts.
- **Always specify `--checkpoint <id>` or `--commit <sha>`** for
  `entire checkpoint explain` — without a locator, the command falls back to an
  interactive picker.

## When No Checkpoints Exist

If the target code predates Entire or has no checkpoint coverage:

1. Say explicitly: "No Entire checkpoint history is available for this code."
2. Proceed with standard code understanding (read source, check git log, trace
   call sites).
3. Label all explanations as "inferred from code — not backed by recorded
   intent."
4. If the user wants deeper history, suggest `search` with related keywords —
   there may be checkpoints on related work even if the specific file isn't
   directly covered.

## Transparency Principle

Always make it clear whether your answer comes from:

- **Checkpoint-backed history** — you read the actual session transcript and
  know the developer's stated intent
- **Code inference** — you analyzed the code structure and are reasoning about
  probable intent

Never present inferred intent as if it were recorded fact. The core value of
this workflow is that distinction.

For a deeper understanding of Entire's capabilities beyond what the sub-skills
cover, consult these resources:

- **CLI help**: run `entire help` to see all available commands and flags
- **Documentation**: https://docs.entire.io/llms.txt — AI-friendly

Make an authenticated HTTP request to an Entire API and print the JSON response.

These endpoints are internal and can change shape without notice; where a
purpose-built command exists, its output is the stable interface.

The CLI attaches the right bearer token and dials the right host for the
chosen backend, so you don't have to plumb auth yourself:

  --to core   the control plane (default): orgs, repos, mirrors, clusters, /me
  --to cell   your home entire-api cell: /me/* activity, repo aggregates

Use --jurisdiction <slug> (e.g. us, eu) to reach a specific jurisdiction's
entire-api cell instead of your home one; it implies --to cell.

<path> is the full path on that host, e.g. /api/v1/clusters. These
placeholders are filled from the current repo's origin remote:
  {owner} {repo}   the GitHub owner / repo
  {repo_id}        the repo's Entire ULID (from its mirror) — cells key on this

The method is GET unless a field/body is given (then POST); override with -X.

When to use this:
LAST RESORT. Right in two cases: you are developing against Entire's own
APIs and want a raw response, or no first-class command covers your need.
Otherwise prefer the command built for the job (checkpoint, session, trail,
status, repo, …) — its output is stable, raw endpoints are not. If you are
reaching for this during ordinary work in a repo with Entire enabled, run
`entire agent-help` first; there is probably a command for it. When you do
need it, use this rather than hand-rolling curl — it attaches the right
bearer and dials the right host for you.

Examples:
entire api /api/v1/clusters
  entire api --to cell /api/v1/me/activity
  entire api --jurisdiction eu /api/v1/me/activity
  entire api --to cell "/api/v1/me/recap?repo={repo_id}"
  entire api -X POST /api/v1/projects -f name=demo

  -i, --include                 print the response status line and headers too

Make an authenticated HTTP request to an Entire API and print the JSON response.

These endpoints are internal and can change shape without notice; where a
purpose-built command exists, its output is the stable interface.

The CLI attaches the right bearer token and dials the right host for the
chosen backend, so you don't have to plumb auth yourself:

  --to core   the control plane (default): orgs, repos, mirrors, clusters, /me
  --to cell   your home entire-api cell: /me/* activity, repo aggregates

Use --jurisdiction <slug> (e.g. us, eu) to reach a specific jurisdiction's
entire-api cell instead of your home one; it implies --to cell.

<path> is the full path on that host, e.g. /api/v1/clusters. These
placeholders are filled from the current repo's origin remote:
  {owner} {repo}   the GitHub owner / repo
  {repo_id}        the repo's Entire ULID (from its mirror) — cells key on this

The method is GET unless a field/body is given (then POST); override with -X.

LAST RESORT. Right in two cases: you are developing against Entire's own

status, repo, …) — its output is stable, raw endpoints are not. If you are
reaching for this during ordinary work in a repo with Entire enabled, run
`entire agent-help` first; there is probably a command for it. When you do
need it, use this rather than hand-rolling curl — it attaches the right
bearer and dials the right host for you.

Entire-Checkpoint: 01M20WKP3K1WHFNEQGKFVEBCFM","sha":"dbe0d142c114c71983564790dbf78fd3f0b37691"},{"author":"Paulo Gomes","date":"2026-09-08T13:37:21Z","login":"pjbgf","message":"checkpoint/remote: require checkpoint_remote ownership for fetches, matching pushes

PushURL confirms a configured checkpoint_remote is ours before routing
writes to it; FetchURL now applies the same check before routing reads,
so an inherited setting cannot select the repository that local
checkpoint refs are populated from. The fetch side's identity set is
origin plus the caller-supplied read candidate, reusing the push side's
predicate so the two directions cannot drift, and a candidate that
fails to resolve counts as unconfirmed ownership rather than being
silently omitted from the set. On an inherited setting, resolution
falls back to the read-candidate chain and the URL is not certified
authoritative, keeping ref-absence classification unaffected.

This deliberately reverses the behavior two tests pinned as "reading
checkpoints is always allowed", and the blast radius is wider than fork
clones: an identity whose owner cannot be determined counts as
inherited, so a repo with a non-forge origin (file://, a bare path, an
unrecognized host) loses a committed checkpoint_remote in both
directions. Declaring the same checkpoint_remote in
.entire/settings.local.json is the escape hatch, as it already was for
pushes, and `entire status` (text and --json) now names the rejected
remote and the ownership reason so the fallback is visible rather than
experienced as checkpoints silently vanishing.

investigate.always_prompt, review prompts, and review profile tasks are
placed verbatim in prompts for agents that run with approvals disabled,
so they get the same provenance requirement as the OPF command and
external_agents: present in .entire/settings.local.json and that file

in .git/ and cannot arrive by cloning. Task and prompt are adjacent
sections of the same composed prompt, so gating one without the other

and runs on the profile task) and is surfaced on stderr rather than
failing the load; the notice stays quiet for a dropped task equal to
the built-in default, which the non-interactive first-run setup
persists into the project file.

Deliberately ungated, each with a mechanism or reason: skills are
validated against the installed set before spawning, agent and model
are registry keys and routing hints, and review_default_profile only
selects among profiles whose instruction content is itself gated.

allow_symlinked_agent_dirs never applied on Windows. The policy is scoped
to the worktree it was loaded for, and the two sides reach that directory
by different routes: readers pass paths.WorktreeRoot, which is git's
`rev-parse --show-toplevel` verbatim and prints forward slashes (C:/repo),
while settings derives its root from entiredir.PathTo, whose filepath.Join
re-Cleans the same path with backslashes (C:\repo). isVouched compared the
two raw strings, so one directory produced two keys and a verified local
grant decided nothing. Hook install, scaffolding, doctor and status all
went on refusing the link, with no diagnostic -- "refused" is also exactly
what an absent grant looks like, which is the indistinguishability
SymlinkedAgentDirsRejection exists to prevent, arrived at by another route.

Canonicalizing would fix the instance. The key is now a distinct TYPE as
well, worktreeKey, built only by keyFor, so comparing a raw path against a
stored key does not compile:

  invalid operation: vouchedForRoot == worktreeRoot
  (mismatched types worktreeKey and string)

That matters more than the tests do here, because the platform this breaks
on is not the platform CI runs. keyFor applies Abs (which also Cleans),
ToSlash, and lowercasing on Windows, where two spellings differing only in
case are one directory. Symlinks are deliberately not resolved: both
producers arrive through git, which has already resolved them, so
EvalSymlinks would buy nothing and could fail on a tree being torn down.

Tests cover the filepath.Join round trip and other spellings on every
platform, that distinct worktrees still key distinctly, and that case
folding is Windows-only. A //go:build windows file pins the literal
C:/repo versus C:\repo shapes; it will not run in this repo's Linux CI,
which is the reason the type exists.

Two rounds of review: a fourth instance of the "creates the thing while
reporting the error" bug plus two smaller items, and three findings from a
codex review of the whole branch.

plugin_index was the fourth unchecked consumer of userdirs.Cache(). With a
relative XDG_CACHE_HOME, SyncPluginIndex created the directory and took a
flock beside it -- both in the working directory -- and got as far as
attempting a clone before osroot.Shared refused the path.
pluginIndexCacheDir now calls a new userdirs.CacheDirChecked and returns
the error first.

The more useful half of that is structural. Config()'s doc comment had
enumerated its consumers twice and been wrong both times: the token store
slipped past the first and plugin_index past the second, the latter in a
comment rewritten one commit earlier to be more careful. Prose cannot fail
when someone adds a caller. The enumeration is gone and
TestUserDirConsumersAreAudited replaces it, requiring every call site of
Config() or Cache() to carry the reason it is safe. Converting a caller to
the *Checked resolver removes it from that ledger, since it is then safe
by construction; the list is meant to shrink, and did so immediately when
the guard failed on plugin_index's own entry.

errSelectionNotPersistable had been inserted between
autoSelectSummaryProvider's doc comment and the function, leaving the
function undocumented under a comment describing the var. Moved.

The vouched-symlink policy is now scoped to the worktree it was loaded
for. It has to be a package global -- settings may import agent, not the
reverse -- and unscoped it let last-load-wins decide for a process that
loads settings for one tree and writes an agent config for another.
Mismatch now refuses, degrading to the strict behaviour rather than to
following another tree's link. This is a different question from why
vouchableDirs is pinned: that is the set a user MAY name and must not be
widenable at runtime; this is the set a user DID name, which is
per-configuration and has to come from somewhere mutable.

From the codex review, all three confirmed by reproduction first:

Doctor stopped scanning at a vouched link, so with .claude vouched and
.claude/skills a link inside the target it reported the one path that is
fine and nothing about the one that is not -- while scaffold installation
genuinely fails there with "skills: path component is a symlink".
scanBeneathVouchedDir resumes the scan from the link's target through
agent.OpenAnchoredRoot, the same resolution the writers use.

Status said "Following symlinked agent directories" from the
CONFIGURATION, so a vouched path that is an ordinary directory, absent, or
dangling was reported as followed. agent.FollowedSymlinkedDirs answers the
question status is actually asking.

The hooks-path remedy interpolated an unquoted path into a command
presented for pasting. A directory containing a space is ordinary, and
`git config core.hooksPath /tmp/my hooks dir` fails with "error: no action
specified". Both print sites now share strategy.HooksPathCommand, whose
POSIX branch delegates to this file's existing shellQuote rather than
repeating the escaping -- the first attempt reimplemented it twelve lines
from the original and got the escape wrong.

Vouching for .pi/extensions/entire was accepted and then made `entire
disable` refuse: OpenHookConfig anchors the root on a followed link's
target, so the stored name collapsed from
.pi/extensions/entire/index.ts to index.ts, and RemoveDir -- which reads
that name to decide which directory it may delete -- saw path.Dir of "."
and reported "refusing to remove the worktree root" about a path that was
neither. Pi discovers extensions by directory, so the refusal left one it
still loads.

Two things were wrong, and both are fixed.

The coordinates. HookConfigFile now carries the worktree-relative name
alongside the root-relative one, the same split entiredir.Name draws:
relName answers questions ABOUT the path, name is for access THROUGH it.
RemoveDir decides its precondition on relName and removes on name.
Reading one coordinate for both jobs is what let anchoring change the
ownership verdict.

The policy. .pi/extensions/entire should never have been vouchable.
It is the one directory Entire both creates and deletes, so it cannot
also be a link the user manages -- the two claims are incompatible, and
the hatch is for the agent's own directory rather than for Entire's
scratch space inside it. neverVouchable now refuses any path whose base is
`entire`, and the pinned list omits it. A user who symlinks it gets the
pre-existing refusal at Write, which is actionable, instead of a
successful install that cannot be uninstalled.

That leaves RemoveDir's anchored-at-the-owned-directory branch
unreachable. It is kept with an accurate message rather than deleted: the
misleading worktree-root claim must not come back if some future path
anchors there.

Vouching .pi or .pi/extensions is unaffected and now has an end-to-end
test at both levels covering install and uninstall, asserting the user's
own link and its target survive. The drift guard grew a
deliberatelyUnvouchable ledger carrying the reason, in the style of
allowedRootBases, and fails three ways: missing entry, stale entry, and
exclusion not enforced.

The second review comment on this pass, about userdirs.Config()/Cache()
absolutizing the home-failure fallback so downstream
RequireAbsoluteOverride checks only see genuine overrides, is already
implemented in 77e65b2a5 via ownFallbackDir. No change needed.

Five review findings on the per-user-directory and summary-provider work.
Only one needed a behaviour change; the others needed coverage that

r3952604662 is the behaviour change, and it is a regression the
absolute-path checks introduced. configDir and cacheDir fall back to
.config/entire and .cache/entire when os.UserHomeDir fails, and the new
checks in contexts.FilePath and withCacheFileLock refused that alongside a
genuine user override. On a machine with no resolvable home -- no HOME, an
odd container, a service account -- every command touching a saved login
or a discovery cache started failing with advice about an environment
variable the user had never set. userdirs.ownFallbackDir absolutizes the
fallback at the one layer that still knows the difference between a value
the user set and one Entire made up: by the time a consumer has a plain
string it cannot tell them apart, which is why the check could not live
only there. Relative user overrides are still refused, in both variables.

r3952596266 and r3952596293 were already enforced ahead of every
MkdirAll, chmod and lock, but only Load and Save had tests. All four
contexts entry points and all four discovery entry points are covered
now, asserting an EMPTY working directory rather than merely an absent
target -- the lock file is created beside the target, so it would land in
the cwd too. LoadCache bypasses withCacheFileLock entirely and reaches the
same verdict by its own route, which the test pins.

r3952596300 was correct in behaviour and wrong in its documentation. The
token store does open an os.Root; the claim that it had none was false.
The reason it needs its own check is that fileStore.dir anchors on
filepath.Dir of its own path and gets there through filepath.Abs, so a
relative config dir is laundered into a plausible absolute path before the
root exists -- the same laundering removed from contexts and discovery.
Documented as that, and the regression coverage now runs through
Get/Set/Delete rather than the internal resolver, with an explicit
ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE_PATH shown to be unaffected.

r3952604655 was a test that proved less than it appeared to. The round
trip ran in one process, where the first call leaves the plugin registered
process-wide, so the second resolution succeeded from memory whatever had
been persisted. It now restores the registry snapshot before resolving
again, which is what a fresh process has; reintroducing the persist makes
it fail, where before it passed. A negative control writes the old broken
state by hand and asserts it is unusable, so the reason not-persisting is
the fix is pinned rather than asserted.

Entire-Checkpoint: 01M20PKEE73AZEJ7MBJY3ES6NA","sha":"a356b917fe858ce8f2c407d7cbc4b165d7c9a26d"},{"author":"Paulo Gomes","date":"2026-09-08T14:06:11Z","login":"pjbgf","message":"test: fix three holes in the git grep source guards

Four tests scan this repo's own source with `git grep` to enforce an
invariant the compiler cannot. Three flags matter, no guard had all three,
and the same one was missing from three of them.

--untracked, because git grep searches the INDEX. Every one of these
guards has "someone just added a file" as its subject, so the file it most
needs to see is the one not yet staged. Two shapes were worse than a miss:
the hook-config guard compares two sets built from the same blind grep, so
a new agent package calling OpenHookConfig without declaring
HookConfigRelPath was absent from both sides and the comparison passed;
and the root-base guard's staleness half reported a just-added entry as
STALE, telling the author to delete the entry that legitimises their new
root. That one reproduced while committing the change before this one.

--no-color, because color.ui or color.grep set to `always` colorizes even
into a pipe and the escapes land in the filename field. True of -l too,
which looks immune, being nothing but filenames. Guards then either
misparse -- read as staleness, which happened on main (#2248) -- or
compare garbage to garbage while their "did we match anything" assertion
still passes.

Repo-selector scrubbing, because git exports GIT_DIR / GIT_WORK_TREE to
the hooks it runs and those outrank cmd.Dir, so a `go test` under a hook
or a `git rebase --exec` scanned a different repository. RunGit's
isolation does not cover this: it filters GIT_CONFIG_* only.

Consolidated into testutil.GitGrepGuard so the reasoning lives once
rather than in four places that had already drifted apart.

Three guard-specific fixes alongside it. The transcript-read ratchet
counted `git grep -c`, which counts LINES containing a match, so a second
read added to a line that already had one was invisible; it now counts
matches with -o. The git status guard's bare `cmd internal` pathspec also
matched testdata .jsonl fixtures and a .md file, so its non-.go branch had
to skip rather than fail -- and that skip was the only thing standing
between colorized output and a guard that silently checked nothing;
narrowed to *.go so the parse failure can be fatal. And
metadata_guard_test.go, a fifth guard that audits git rev-parse call sites
by AST rather than by grep, gets an audited-query entry for the new
helper.

Verified against a hostile local color.ui=always, a decoy GIT_DIR, and
untracked probe files planted for two of the guards.

was to stop managing it that way.

allow_symlinked_agent_dirs in .entire/settings.local.json names
worktree-relative agent config directories whose symlinks are followed,
anchoring the root on the resolved target. Three properties keep it a
hatch rather than a hole.

It is a list, not a boolean: a flag disables the class, where naming a
path says which arrangement is the user's.

It has two independent boundaries. The same untracked-and-verified gate as
the OPF command and external_agents decides whether the FILE may grant --
a repository that could both ship the link and vouch for it is the whole
attack. A name check then decides whether the PATH is one an agent config
lives under, so .entire and .git/hooks are unspellable even from a
verified local file.

And the vouchable set is pinned rather than derived from
AllHookConfigRelPaths, which was the first version and was wrong twice:
that registry is mutable at runtime, so deriving would let an external
plugin widen what a user can be persuaded to vouch for, and it is empty in
a binary that has not imported the agent packages, so the set collapsed
depending on the caller's import graph.
TestVouchableDirsMatchTheBuiltInAgents catches drift both ways.

Vouching for a directory does not vouch for links inside it: below the
anchor everything is a name in a root again. The skill scaffolds go
through the same anchor, or enable half-applies across two directories. A
vouched but unresolvable link is an error, not a quiet fall back to
refusing. status prints what is followed and what was rejected, and doctor
reports it as FOLLOWING SYMLINKS rather than as a fault.

.entire, the settings files and the git hooks directory are deliberately
excluded. The settings case is circular -- a symlinked settings.local.json
vouching for symlinked settings files authorizes itself -- and the hooks
case already has git's own core.hooksPath.

introduced rather than gaps they left.

and detection, so a symlinked hooks directory could not be uninstalled
past -- RemoveGitHook is the only uninstall path -- while

persistSummaryProviderSelection still wrote it down -- Entire breaking

registered already, and the next run re-selects the same provider.

a filename is often a legal branch name -- so pass a trailing `--`.

The `sh -c` in realRunInstaller is a considered exception to "never put a
dynamic value on a shell line", not an oversight: updateCommand returns one
of five compile-time literals, the binary's path and version choose between
them rather than appearing inside them, and the shell is load-bearing for
the fallback, which is a pipeline (`curl … | bash`). Rewriting that as argv
means re-implementing the pipe, which is more moving parts than the risk it
removes.

That reasoning holds only while the literals stay literal, and the tempting
next change is the one that breaks it — interpolating the channel, the
version, or the Scoop app name into the command, which would look entirely
reasonable in review. So enforce it: drive every install manager and
channel with adversarial exec paths and versions, and fail when the result
is not one of the known strings.

are there so a future interpolation surfaces as a failing test rather than
as a quoting question nobody thinks to ask.

The active hooks directory was the last tree Entire wrote to with bare
os.ReadFile/os.WriteFile on a joined path. A symlink at a hook path was
therefore read through and then written through: the 0o755 os.WriteFile
truncated whatever the link named and replaced it with a shell script.

Anchor a root at git's own `--git-path hooks` answer, refusing a symlink at
the directory itself; route the four hook reads through
osroot.ReadFileNoFollow; and replace the write with
jsonutil.WriteFileAtomicIn, whose rename replaces a leaf link instead of
following it. osroot.OpenFileNoFollow is deliberately not used for the
write: it rejects O_TRUNC by design, precisely to push truncating writes
onto an atomic rename.

The hooks directory needs its own anchor rather than an existing one
because core.hooksPath can name any directory, inside the worktree or well
outside it, so allowedRootBases gains an entry with that reason.

A symlinked hook is now classified as foreign rather than as absent, so it
is backed up to <hook>.pre-entire and chained to exactly as a foreign
script is. Refusing to read through someone's link must not mean silently
discarding it, and the rename preserves the link itself as the backup.

doctor grows checkGitHookSymlinks, reporting a symlinked hooks directory
(which stops installation, and is otherwise invisible: every other command
just reports the hooks absent) and a symlinked hook file (which is not an
error, only a surprise worth naming). It is a separate function from
checkAgentDirSymlinks because that one scans worktree-relative paths
through the worktree root, and core.hooksPath can point outside the
worktree.

`entire session current` answered "which session state moved most recently, preferring this worktree" and described it as "the active session for the current worktree". Worktrees share one session store, so in a worktree with no sessions of its own it silently fell back across the whole store and returned a live session belonging to somewhere else — that worktree's path right there in the JSON, indistinguishable from a real answer.

That is not a cosmetic mislabel. Agents reach for this command to find their own session id, read the id back, and pass it to `entire session adopt`, which moves the named session into the current worktree and resets its checkpoint bookkeeping. A wrong id there mutates a third party's running session.

Five agents already publish their session id into the environment of the processes they spawn, and Entire read none of them. `strategy.ResolveCallerSession` now answers the question directly, in tiers, each reported back so a caller can tell an identification from a guess: `caller-env` (the agent named it), `ancestry` (a session's recorded Owner is our ancestor — the same match commit linking performs, which is what covers the agents that publish nothing), `worktree`, then `other-worktree`. The weak tiers stay, because "what has been happening in this repo" is a real question; they just have to say that is what they answered. `SessionResolution.IsCaller()` is the gate for acting on a session rather than displaying it.

Three call sites, all of which were asking the caller question: `session current`, a bare `session tokens`, and the hook log-stamp in `withHookSession` — an agent-triggered git hook inherits the agent's variable, so log lines now name the session that ran the commit instead of whichever one moved last. `FindMostRecentSession` is untouched and serves as the bottom tiers.

The per-agent half is declarative: an agent implements `CallerSessionIdentifier` by naming its variable, and the `agent` package does the read, so the id is validated with `validation.ValidateAgentSessionID` in exactly one place. That is load-bearing rather than tidy — the id becomes a path component in `ResolveSessionFile`, so an unvalidated one out of the environment is a traversal sink. Declaring the name instead of the value also makes the set enumerable, which is what lets tests clear it.

Every variable was established against the shipped agent rather than inferred: Claude Code `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID`, Codex `CODEX_SESSION_ID` (the root-session identity — not `CODEX_THREAD_ID`, which follows forks and subagent threads), Cursor `CURSOR_CONVERSATION_ID`, Copilot CLI `COPILOT_AGENT_SESSION_ID`, pi `PI_SESSION_ID`. Gemini CLI and opencode publish nothing, which is a finding rather than a gap: Gemini passes its session id only to its own background-process bookkeeping, and opencode's shell tool augments no environment at all. That is why the ancestry tier is not optional.

Two states are kept distinct on the caller tier. An id the agent named but Entire holds no state for is reported as a diagnosis — "you are in session X and Entire is not recording it" — rather than falling through and answering with an unrelated session. And several claims at once is the normal nested case (a `codex exec` under Claude Code sees both variables), resolved by ancestry depth, then by recency.

The test harnesses now clear these variables, and that is not incidental: three existing tests failed while writing this because the developer's own agent session leaked into a spawned binary, which is the same class of failure the config/cache isolation in both TestMains exists to prevent. Derived from the registry so it cannot rot when an agent gains the capability.

A finding on #2309 claimed the three CheckAndNotify tests moved there fail when
a developer has MISE_INSTALLS_DIR set wide enough to cover brewCaskPath (it
suggested /opt). The premise is right and the conclusion is not: both probes
match, but UpdateCommandForCurrentBinary returns the FIRST match and
installProbes orders brewProbe ahead of miseProbe, so brew wins.

    miseProbe.matches("/opt/homebrew/Caskroom/entire/1.0.0/entire") = true
    brewProbe.matches("/opt/homebrew/Caskroom/entire/1.0.0/entire") = true
    UpdateCommandForCurrentBinary() = "brew upgrade --yes entire"

Confirmed against every MISE_INSTALLS_DIR worth trying, /opt and / included,
plus MISE_DATA_DIR. The comparison to 73a3d39 does not hold either: that fixed
the two table rows whose expectation is the *fallback*, where by definition no
probe matched, so precedence could not rescue them. Here it does.

What the finding did surface is that precedence is load-bearing and unpinned.
It is a product invariant, not just test scaffolding: someone can have entire
installed by brew and mise relocated under a broad root, and that user has to
be told to run brew. Reordering installProbes would silently change the advice,
and would break those tests only on the developer boxes that set the variable.

So pin it, asserting the precondition as well as the outcome — without a
contending probe the test would keep passing while testing nothing. Verified by
mutation: flipping installProbes fails on the outcome, and stopping mise
matching fails on the precondition.

Also fold isolateMiseInstallEnv into newAutoUpdateFixture, which is already
where a test's environment is made hermetic (HOME, kill switch, TTY), and into
the one test that wires the same seams inline instead of using the fixture.
That is decoupling rather than a fix — nothing was failing — so that the tests
no longer depend on precedence at all, and the invariant is asserted in one
place that says why.

A named pipe at a path Entire reads hung the process instead of failing it.
open(2) on a FIFO with no writer blocks until one arrives, and none of the
NoFollow helpers passes O_NONBLOCK, so in a repo with a FIFO at
.claude/settings.json:

    mkdir -p .claude && mkfifo .claude/settings.json && entire doctor
    # prints "Metadata branches: OK", then blocks in openat. SIGINT only.

    os.(*Root).Open                 root.go:103
    osroot.OpenNoFollow             osroot/osroot.go:80   <- parent.Open, no O_NONBLOCK
    agent.(*HookConfigFile).Read    agent/hook_config_file.go:112
    claudecode.loadClaudeSettings   claudecode/hooks.go:433
    claudecode.CheckHookConfig      claudecode/hooks.go:499

OpenNoFollow already Lstats the leaf to reject a symlink, so the type check goes
in the same place and costs nothing. Being BEFORE the open is the whole point: a
post-open check cannot help, because the open is what blocks.

Directories are refused too. io.ReadAll of one already failed a step later with
a platform-dependent errno, and a caller asking for a file wants the refusal
rather than an EISDIR from the middle of its read.

Scope, measured rather than assumed:

- `entire doctor` hangs. `entire status` and `entire agent list` do NOT — they
  reach the config through Exists (an Lstat), not Read. The exposure is narrower
  than "every command that reads an agent config", which is what I first wrote.
- `git status --porcelain` does not list a FIFO at all, so the checkpoint path
  that reads working files from status output was never exposed.
- Every read funnels through here, so the fix covers all nine agents plus
  permissions.go, the plugin manifest, doctor's log readers and the settings
  loader. Verified no caller wants a non-regular file: the one that reads from a
  directory listing (review/manifest.go:737) already skips entry.IsDir().

ErrNotRegularFile is deliberately not classified as os.ErrNotExist. Several
callers reach these helpers to decide "is there a config here?", and answering
"absent" for an occupied path would have Entire write a fresh file over whatever
is there. A missing file still classifies as before, which a test pins.

fs.ModeIrregular is masked out rather than matched, the same tolerance the
.entire entry scan applies: Windows maps uncategorised reparse tags onto that
bit, which lands OneDrive Files On-Demand placeholders there, and a placeholder
is a readable file.

The FIFO test races the open against a timer instead of asserting on its error,
because a regression does not fail here — it hangs, and a plain assertion would
take the package's timeout with it.

type in doctor's scan but could not stop the hang. Independent of it: no shared
files, either can land first.

readCapped's cap is a byte budget, applied as `s[:maxLen]`, while both callers'
constants describe it in characters:

    tuneDocCap    = 6000 // max chars embedded per doc (CLAUDE.md etc.)
    tuneReadmeCap = 2000

So a CLAUDE.md whose 6000th byte falls inside a multi-byte rune put an invalid
UTF-8 sequence into the prompt `entire runner tune` sends to a model. Nothing
downstream validates, so it was invisible from the call site.

A continuation byte at the cut is exactly what "we cut mid-rune" means, so the
fix backs off the continuation bytes — at most UTFMax-1 of them, which is the
furthest a rune's start can be. `utf8.RuneStart` answers that from one byte,
where validating the prefix walks the whole 6KB and answers a different question:
"is this valid?" is false for a doc that is not UTF-8 at all, and chasing it back
drops the file's content in favour of a bare truncation marker. Invalidity our
cut did not cause is the file's own, and the under-cap path passes those bytes
through too.

Two traps, both pinned by tests rather than described:

- A latin-1 README came back as just the truncation marker when the backoff had
  no bound, which is worse than the mid-rune cut it was fixing.
- The floor has to be explicit rather than implied by an iteration count. At
  maxLen=1 over a file of continuation bytes, a count-based bound indexes s[-1]
  and panics — latent, since the smallest cap any caller passes is go.mod's 400.

First tests for readCapped: the boundary itself, a short file, a missing one, a
non-UTF-8 doc keeping its content, and every cap from 0 to 7 over three body
shapes asserting the contract as a disjunction — the cut lands on a rune
boundary, or it keeps the file's own bytes. An empty result is correct below one
rune's width, where no non-empty valid prefix exists.

Split out of the os.Root coverage follow-ups (#2290): a byte cap cutting a rune
in prompt text is unrelated to filesystem anchoring, and this is the piece of
that branch that stands alone.

timeout, but only opencode read it — so on the other nine runners the variable
moved nothing. Two of the ten also disagreed with the documented 2m default

overrides in split_commits_test.go and multi_session_test.go no-ops for half
the matrix.

duration (cursor derives an absolute deadline, codex/copilot-cli/gemini a
separate promptCtx), and boundPrompt for those that just want a bounded ctx.
TestEveryRunPromptResolvesThroughPromptTimeout fails the build on a runner that
resolves its own, since both failure modes are invisible at runtime — you get a
run that ignores the budget you set.

roger-roger get no per-prompt default, keeping the ForEachAgent scenario
timeout as their only deadline; imposing the documented 2m on them would be a

validate. E2E_TIMEOUT and WithPromptTimeout now bound them when asked.

default: ignoring it is how you widen a budget, watch the run fail at the old
ceiling, and blame the agent.

per-runner defaults and say which runners have none.

The backoff ran a fixed UTFMax-1 passes with no lower bound, so at maxLen=1 over
a file of continuation bytes the third pass indexed s[-1]:

    readCapped(dir, "go.mod", 1) over "\x80\x80..."
    panic: runtime error: index out of range [-1]

Introduced by 36daaea18, which swapped a whole-prefix utf8.ValidString for
utf8.RuneStart at the cut. The count-based bound was safe with ValidString —
s[:0] is a legal slice — and became an out-of-range index once it was used to
subscript. Found by Copilot and by the trail's own review, both on the same
line. No caller passes a cap this small (the smallest is go.mod's 400), so it
was latent, which is the reason to pin it rather than to shrug.

The floor is now explicit (`max(0, maxLen-(utf8.UTFMax-1))`) instead of implied
by an iteration count, and a rune start that never turns up leaves the cut at
maxLen — so the file's own bytes are kept rather than dropped, which is what the
preceding commit was about.

Behaviour at every cap 0..7, over an all-continuation body, a
continuation-prefixed body and a valid two-byte-rune body: no panic; the cut
lands on a rune boundary or keeps the file's bytes; an empty result only below
one rune's width, where no non-empty valid prefix exists. The test asserts that
disjunction rather than "not empty", because "" is the correct answer at
maxLen=1 over a 2-byte rune — an earlier draft of it asserted non-empty and was
wrong about the contract.

Quality pass over the preceding six commits. No behaviour change except where
noted; two of these close gaps the first versions left open.

**Two guards were unsound.**

`scanForSymlinkedComponent` tested `Type() == 0` for "a regular file where a
directory belongs", which is a blocklist of one: a FIFO, socket or device node
at `.claude` came back clean and doctor printed nothing, while os.Root and every
hook install fail on it. Now an allowlist of the traversable shapes
(`traversableComponent`), which is what the .entire scan's doc argues for at
length — an allowlist a rejected type can enter by setting an extra bit is not
an allowlist. fs.ModeIrregular stays tolerated: a Windows junction arrives as
bare ModeIrregular and a cloud placeholder directory as ModeDir|ModeIrregular,
and both are traversable.

`RemoveDir` refused an `AllProtectedDirs()` entry, which is a blocklist and
misses the case that matters: that list holds `.opencode` and `.github/hooks`
but not `.opencode/plugins`, `.pi/extensions` or `.github`, so a future agent
whose config sits one level below its root still got
`RemoveAll(".opencode/plugins")` — the user's other plugins. Stated positively
instead: the directory has to be one Entire named. Every agent root and shared
intermediate fails that; pi's `.pi/extensions/entire` passes because Entire
created it.

**Duplication.**

`printCappedList` replaces four inline copies of the same capped-list loop in
doctor.go (three added by 761b87d68, one pre-existing in
checkEntireDirSymlinks), so the off-by-one truncation contract is written once.
`testutil.SkipWithoutSymlinks` replaces six copies of the Windows symlink skip
in three different wordings. `agentHelpSkillTemplate` is back to one switch on
agentName, so a fourth agent cannot get a path with no body. The three
worktreeFileName tests are one table, which also makes them agree visibly with
worktreedir's four cases one layer down — and writing it out caught a wrong
expectation of mine: a RELATIVE in-repo link never reaches the resolve, because
os.Root follows it, so the fast path returns the original name.

**Waste and dead state.**

readCapped asked `utf8.ValidString` over the whole 6KB prefix up to four times
to find a rune boundary; `utf8.RuneStart` at the cut answers the same question
by looking at one byte (2081ns -> 2ns measured) and removes the whole-prefix
fallback with it. A new test pins the floor, since a file of nothing but
continuation bytes must still keep its content.

guarded was skipped — so the name is now the sole presence signal and
`loadVercelConfigIfPresent` says out loud that no vercel.json means nothing to

RemoveDir's doc says every other agent must not call it, because "taking the
parent would delete the user's own config with it". The only guard was
dir == ".", and path.Dir is .claude for .claude/settings.json, .cursor for
.cursor/hooks.json, .codex for .codex/hooks.json — so a second caller got

the only caller today; the hazard is a copy-paste during the next agent
integration. It now refuses a directory that is an AllProtectedDirs() entry,
which is the same argument the HookConfigLocator build guard makes: a
precondition this load-bearing belongs in the code.

Write's error message used path.Dir on f.path, an OS-separated absolute path. On
Windows that has no forward slashes, so the message named "." instead of the
directory. filepath.Dir, as the two arms beside it already use.

The guard test compared len(declared) against len(callers). Counts passed
whenever an added omission was offset by a removal in the same change — the
exact failure it exists to catch, since the agent still works and only doctor's
diagnosis goes quiet — and would fail on an agent whose call sits in a
sub-package, which is no defect. It now compares the set of packages calling
OpenHookConfig against the set implementing HookConfigRelPath (eight each), plus

own failure.

line carried a note saying pi reads the directory. Keeping 0750, and saying so —
the eight other agents have been on 0750 all along and pi is not structurally
different, since it runs as whoever ran `entire enable`. A setup where those
differ breaks all nine equally and is not pi's to fix here.

Four things in checkAgentDirSymlinks, all of them cases where the check went
quiet or said the wrong thing.

A regular file at .claude made Lstat(".claude/settings.json") return ENOTDIR,
which is not ENOENT, so it landed in componentScanUnreadable and doctor answered
"check the ownership and permissions" for a condition only replacing the path
fixes. That is the else-branch pattern CLAUDE.md's .entire section separates
ErrEntireDirNotDirectory from ErrEntireDirUnreadable to avoid, and for the same
reason: the two remedies are different things. componentScanWrongType reports it
under BROKEN with the replace remedy. Identified from the parent's own mode —
Type() == 0 is positively a regular file — rather than by matching an errno,
and fs.ModeIrregular is left out of that test the way the .entire scan leaves it
out, since Windows lands junctions and cloud placeholders on the same bit.

.claude/agents/ was in no candidate. removeLegacySearchSubagent deletes
.claude/agents/entire-search.md through osroot.LstatNoSymlinks, which refuses a
symlinked parent — its own doc says .claude/agents/ arrives with a checkout — so
a link there was refused at enable with a best-effort warning and doctor said
nothing. .codex/agents and .gemini/agents were covered already, but only as a
side effect of the agent-help template living under them; legacySearchSubagentPath
is now a source in its own right.

A worktree root that would not open returned bare, printing nothing at all on a
repo where every hook install also fails. It reports NOT CHECKED, which is the
stance the per-component path twelve lines down already takes.

searchSkillTemplatePath and agentHelpSkillTemplatePath split the location out of
the template builders. The candidate scan wants nineteen paths and was trimming
and copying twelve multi-KB bodies to get them, then discarding the bytes.

Also records why the list is not gated on the agent being configured: .github
and .agents are shared user-owned trees, so a monorepo symlinking either is told
about it even when those agents are off. Gating would have to ask whether hooks
are installed, and that question is answered by reading through the very config
a symlink hides, so the check would fall silent exactly where it is needed.

708f78136 moved Vercel detection onto the worktree root and said in two places
that an in-repo symlink is still followed, because pointing vercel.json at a
monorepo's shared config is a real setup and the file is the user's rather than

unconditionally, even one landing inside the root, and the error is not

    root.Stat("vercel.json")      err=statat vercel.json: path escapes from parent

repo where it worked before the anchor went in. CLAUDE.md already records this

symlink-following billy.Basic.

worktreeFileName tries the root first and, on a refusal that is not "absent",
resolves through worktreedir.NameFollowingLinks and retries at the resolved
name. That delivers what the comments promised — follow a link that stays
inside, refuse one that leaves — with the retried read still going through the

Entire-Checkpoint: 01M1GPM7287QNEQ1CH466S1DEQ","sha":"4bd4753e68a1d955d94ac23f02be34228e061748"},{"author":"Stefan Haubold","date":"2026-09-02T09:18:47Z","login":"Soph","message":"worktreedir: cover rooted-relative paths, and resolve in-repo links

Two changes to Name's containment answer.

2ddbae3bb paired VolumeName with IsAbs to keep "C:foo" off the name branch.
Windows has a second form of the same shape: "\foo", where volumeNameLen is 0
because a single leading backslash is neither a volume nor a UNC prefix, so
IsAbs is false and VolumeName is empty and the guard passed. filepath.IsLocal is
the single primitive that covers both, and is what os.Root itself uses one layer
down — which is also why neither was a reachable escape. Closed for the reason
the first one was: Name exists to answer "is this inside the worktree?"
independently of the caller.

NameFollowingLinks is new, for the callers whose file is the USER's rather than
Entire's. os.Root refuses an ABSOLUTE symlink target unconditionally, including
one resolving inside the root, so a root alone cannot express "follow a link
that stays in the worktree, refuse one that leaves". It resolves the link, then
answers for the target. The base is resolved too, against the same rules:
without that, every repository below a symlinked component judges its own files
from a path that no longer matches them — on macOS /var is a link to
/private/var, so a worktree under /var/folders/... reported each of its own
files as outside itself.

The name returned is worktree-relative and symlink-free, so the caller's read
still goes through the root and a link repointed in between cannot escape.

Entire-Checkpoint: 01M1GPKVR0RXKEVYMMTY64E5WR","sha":"5ea1fc35112acb51d49ec54116a23e864413723a"},{"author":"Stefan Haubold","date":"2026-09-05T19:13:43Z","login":"Soph","message":"flock: retry an open whose file was replaced, and derace the tests

Two follow-ups to the inode revalidation.

The replaced-inode tests were racy in their polling variants, ~35% under
-race (14/40). The helper unlinked the lock file and then acquired the
replacement, but a polling waiter re-opens with O_CREATE on its next
25ms tick, so the waiter could create the replacement itself, lock it,
revalidate it clean and return holding it - leaving the helper to block
on that inode until its own deadline and fail at "Acquire new lock".
The waiter is behaving correctly; the assumption that the helper wins
the replacement is what was unfounded. installLockedReplacement now
renames an already-locked file over the name, so the name is never
observable unlocked.

That left one failure in 40, from the opener rather than the test.
osroot.validateOpenedFile runs the same SameFile check the revalidation
added, but at open time, and openLockFileIn only retried ErrExist and
ErrNotExist - so a replacement landing after acquire was retried while
one landing inside the opener's window was fatal. The mismatch now
carries the ErrReplacedDuringOpen sentinel and openLockFileIn retries
it, which is the same event its existing loop already covers, just seen
a moment earlier.

Verified: 0/40 under -race (was 14/40); all four revalidation tests
still fail against main, so the derace does not weaken them; under a
tight os.Remove loop against AcquireIn the escaping mismatches drop
from 3471 to 394 (the remainder is the deliberate 3-retry bound).

Entire-Checkpoint: 01M20WKP3K1WHFNEQGKFVEBCFM","sha":"dbe0d142c114c71983564790dbf78fd3f0b37691"},{"author":"Paulo Gomes","date":"2026-09-08T13:37:21Z","login":"pjbgf","message":"checkpoint/remote: require checkpoint_remote ownership for fetches, matching pushes

PushURL confirms a configured checkpoint_remote is ours before routing
writes to it; FetchURL now applies the same check before routing reads,
so an inherited setting cannot select the repository that local
checkpoint refs are populated from. The fetch side's identity set is
origin plus the caller-supplied read candidate, reusing the push side's
predicate so the two directions cannot drift, and a candidate that
fails to resolve counts as unconfirmed ownership rather than being
silently omitted from the set. On an inherited setting, resolution
falls back to the read-candidate chain and the URL is not certified
authoritative, keeping ref-absence classification unaffected.

This deliberately reverses the behavior two tests pinned as "reading
checkpoints is always allowed", and the blast radius is wider than fork
clones: an identity whose owner cannot be determined counts as
inherited, so a repo with a non-forge origin (file://, a bare path, an
unrecognized host) loses a committed checkpoint_remote in both
directions. Declaring the same checkpoint_remote in
.entire/settings.local.json is the escape hatch, as it already was for
pushes, and `entire status` (text and --json) now names the rejected
remote and the ownership reason so the fallback is visible rather than
experienced as checkpoints silently vanishing.

investigate.always_prompt, review prompts, and review profile tasks are
placed verbatim in prompts for agents that run with approvals disabled,
so they get the same provenance requirement as the OPF command and
external_agents: present in .entire/settings.local.json and that file
verified untracked, or set through clone-local preferences, which live
in .git/ and cannot arrive by cloning. Task and prompt are adjacent
sections of the same composed prompt, so gating one without the other
would just move an attacker's text to the other field. Rejection
downgrades the field (a dropped task falls back to the built-in text
for conventional profile names, and a prompt-only worker stays present
and runs on the profile task) and is surfaced on stderr rather than
failing the load; the notice stays quiet for a dropped task equal to
the built-in default, which the non-interactive first-run setup
persists into the project file.

Deliberately ungated, each with a mechanism or reason: skills are
validated against the installed set before spawning, agent and model
are registry keys and routing hints, and review_default_profile only
selects among profiles whose instruction content is itself gated.

applyJSONReplacements splices by matching the re-encoded leaf against the
raw line. JSON admits more than one encoding of the same string, so a
producer's encoding choice could leave a leaf outside the splice's reach
with no signal. Redaction now re-checks every spliced line against the
collected originals and falls back to a structural re-encode of that
line; a line that cannot be rewritten fails the redaction rather than
certifying.

allow_symlinked_agent_dirs never applied on Windows. The policy is scoped
to the worktree it was loaded for, and the two sides reach that directory
by different routes: readers pass paths.WorktreeRoot, which is git's
`rev-parse --show-toplevel` verbatim and prints forward slashes (C:/repo),
while settings derives its root from entiredir.PathTo, whose filepath.Join
re-Cleans the same path with backslashes (C:\repo). isVouched compared the
two raw strings, so one directory produced two keys and a verified local
grant decided nothing. Hook install, scaffolding, doctor and status all
went on refusing the link, with no diagnostic -- "refused" is also exactly
what an absent grant looks like, which is the indistinguishability
SymlinkedAgentDirsRejection exists to prevent, arrived at by another route.

Canonicalizing would fix the instance. The key is now a distinct TYPE as
well, worktreeKey, built only by keyFor, so comparing a raw path against a
stored key does not compile:

  invalid operation: vouchedForRoot == worktreeRoot
  (mismatched types worktreeKey and string)

That matters more than the tests do here, because the platform this breaks
on is not the platform CI runs. keyFor applies Abs (which also Cleans),
ToSlash, and lowercasing on Windows, where two spellings differing only in
case are one directory. Symlinks are deliberately not resolved: both
producers arrive through git, which has already resolved them, so
EvalSymlinks would buy nothing and could fail on a tree being torn down.

Tests cover the filepath.Join round trip and other spellings on every
platform, that distinct worktrees still key distinctly, and that case
folding is Windows-only. A //go:build windows file pins the literal
C:/repo versus C:\repo shapes; it will not run in this repo's Linux CI,
which is the reason the type exists.

Two rounds of review: a fourth instance of the "creates the thing while
reporting the error" bug plus two smaller items, and three findings from a
codex review of the whole branch.

plugin_index was the fourth unchecked consumer of userdirs.Cache(). With a
relative XDG_CACHE_HOME, SyncPluginIndex created the directory and took a
flock beside it -- both in the working directory -- and got as far as
attempting a clone before osroot.Shared refused the path.
pluginIndexCacheDir now calls a new userdirs.CacheDirChecked and returns
the error first.

The more useful half of that is structural. Config()'s doc comment had
enumerated its consumers twice and been wrong both times: the token store
slipped past the first and plugin_index past the second, the latter in a
comment rewritten one commit earlier to be more careful. Prose cannot fail
when someone adds a caller. The enumeration is gone and
TestUserDirConsumersAreAudited replaces it, requiring every call site of
Config() or Cache() to carry the reason it is safe. Converting a caller to
the *Checked resolver removes it from that ledger, since it is then safe
by construction; the list is meant to shrink, and did so immediately when
the guard failed on plugin_index's own entry.

errSelectionNotPersistable had been inserted between
autoSelectSummaryProvider's doc comment and the function, leaving the
function undocumented under a comment describing the var. Moved.

The vouched-symlink policy is now scoped to the worktree it was loaded
for. It has to be a package global -- settings may import agent, not the
reverse -- and unscoped it let last-load-wins decide for a process that
loads settings for one tree and writes an agent config for another.
Mismatch now refuses, degrading to the strict behaviour rather than to
following another tree's link. This is a different question from why
vouchableDirs is pinned: that is the set a user MAY name and must not be
widenable at runtime; this is the set a user DID name, which is
per-configuration and has to come from somewhere mutable.

From the codex review, all three confirmed by reproduction first:

Doctor stopped scanning at a vouched link, so with .claude vouched and
.claude/skills a link inside the target it reported the one path that is
fine and nothing about the one that is not -- while scaffold installation
genuinely fails there with "skills: path component is a symlink".
scanBeneathVouchedDir resumes the scan from the link's target through
agent.OpenAnchoredRoot, the same resolution the writers use.

Status said "Following symlinked agent directories" from the
CONFIGURATION, so a vouched path that is an ordinary directory, absent, or
dangling was reported as followed. agent.FollowedSymlinkedDirs answers the
question status is actually asking.

The hooks-path remedy interpolated an unquoted path into a command
presented for pasting. A directory containing a space is ordinary, and
`git config core.hooksPath /tmp/my hooks dir` fails with "error: no action
specified". Both print sites now share strategy.HooksPathCommand, whose
POSIX branch delegates to this file's existing shellQuote rather than
repeating the escaping -- the first attempt reimplemented it twelve lines
from the original and got the escape wrong.
